latin_text: [From critical edition, p. 85, lines 2968-2977; Pseudo-Dionysius, De mystica theologia V]
english_translation: He is not truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor one, nor unity, nor deity, nor goodness, nor spirit, so far as we can know him, nor does he have the name father or son nor any other of the things which are known to us or to anyone else in the world, nor is he any other of the things which are not nor any of the things which are, nor do the things which are know the divinity as it is, nor does it know the things which are as they are, nor is there any speaking of it, nor name nor science nor darkness nor light, nor error nor truth, neither is there any affirmation or negation of it.
translation_source: Miller translation (Hackett edition, 1998); quoting Pseudo-Dionysius De mystica theologia
exegesis: This passage, the heart of apophatic theology, establishes that God transcends all predicates—being, unity, goodness, and even the negations themselves. The cascade of denials serves not to deprive God of these perfections but to indicate that God infinitely exceeds them. Every created being, including angels, has being, unity, truth, and goodness as participated properties. But God, beyond all names and concepts, cannot be comprehended even by the seraphim. This establishes the apex of the hierarchy: the angelic ladder rises toward a darkness that surpasses light, a unknowing that transcends knowledge. No creature, however exalted, can approach God as He is in Himself. The passage thus frames angelology within the economy of participated being: angels are the highest creatures precisely because they approach this transcendent mystery most closely, yet always fall short.
metaphysical_theme: God's radical transcendence beyond all being, one, and intelligibility; even seraphim cannot know God as God is; angels approach only through radical negation and mystical unknowing

notes: HARVESTER passage U.2.2 is the locus classicus for apophatic theology in Pico's angelology. The extended negation establishes that the hierarchy of being culminates not in divine knowability but in divine mystery. This passage frames all subsequent metaphysical doctrine: participated being is always, ultimately, a participation in something that transcends understanding. Angels exemplify this paradox: they are the highest lights, yet their light illuminates only the unknowability of their source.
